^-marked entries are compressed stubs carrying child addresses. Their narration and any surfaced witness quotes are verbatim-accurate — quote them as-is — but a stub carries no provenance (source, date, supersession). Expand (aswritten_expand with the IRIs you need) before any claim that turns on WHEN or by WHOM something was said, or whether it is still the current framing. Witness-depth sections below already carry full provenance.

Deciding where to go: each mapped area's narration tells you the SPAN of what lives under it; the area index names everything else. Expand a subtree when its narration (or name) shows your subject plausibly lives there — you'll get the trajectory, the variants, and the verbatim witness. But be strict about absence: if neither the map's narrations nor the index's names substantively cover your subject, it is NOT in this perspective — say so rather than expanding a loose thematic match (a word-overlap is not coverage). positions.name: OwnedVsRentedIntelligence
positions.frame: what is the asset that ownership secures, as against the substrate that is merely rented or commoditized?
positions.why: Both expressions perform the same balanced, aphoristic maxim in native technical vocabulary (owned/rented; commodity/asset), both appeal to autonomy and self-enhancement rather than argue from evidence, and both are delivered at principle-level conviction — flat, unhedged, constitutive statements rather than claims held open to revision. Read together they stake out one directional distinction: what is possessed and kept (perspective) versus what is interchangeable and paid for (substrate).

placements.frame: Does this expression treat the underlying substrate/model as interchangeable and commoditized while treating the owned perspective (or individually-owned intelligence) as the thing that is scarce, retained, and defensible?

This is a subject future envelopes about the individually-owned-intelligence thesis will keep feeding (per src-4's own framing as restating an existing thesis), not a one-time fact, so it passes the narrative grain test.
